item.title: Postpartum Depression May Not Start After Birth
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Postpartum Depression May Not Start After Birth

Research shows why timing and symptoms matter with postpartum depression.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Depression symptoms identified postpartum can emerge before pregnancy, during pregnancy, or after birth.
  • Nearly two-thirds of women with postpartum depression have another mental health condition.
  • A positive depression screen in new mothers is reason for further assessment, not a diagnosis.
Source: Vale Marquez / Pexels

While we commonly think of postpartum depression when we think about maternal mental health, there is much more to the story. A seminal study of 10,000 mothers who recently gave birth offers a more complicated, but useful, picture of maternal mental health. Researchers found that among women who screened positive for depression in the postpartum period and then completed a comprehensive diagnostic assessment, their mental health experiences varied considerably. Some women's current psychiatric episodes began after birth, while others began during pregnancy or even before.

In other words, women experiencing postpartum mental health difficulties do not all have the same diagnosis, symptom presentation, or symptom onset. Understanding these differences gives us a more complete picture of maternal mental health.

Onset of Mental Health Symptoms

One of the study's most interesting findings was the diverse onset of symptoms:

  • 40.1 percent in postpartum
  • 33.4 percent during pregnancy
  • 26.5 percent before pregnancy

These findings describe when a woman's current psychiatric episode began, not necessarily when they first experienced the condition. For many women who experience significant mental health symptoms after giving birth, the difficulties actually began earlier. In fact, for nearly 60 percent of the women, the current psychiatric episode identified postpartum actually began before or during pregnancy. Among the women diagnosed with postpartum depression, the majority (65 percent) had recurrent depression, rather than a new onset. However, by the time a mother seeks help postpartum, all of these experiences may simply be described as “postpartum depression.”

Source: Helena Lopes / Pexels

Depression Isn't the Whole Story

The researchers also found that a positive screen on a commonly used perinatal depression screening tool (i.e., the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, EDPS) did not necessarily mean a woman had depression. Instead, among the women who completed an extensive follow-up psychiatric interview, the primary diagnoses were:

  • 68.5 percent with depression
  • 22.6 percent with bipolar disorder
  • 5.6 percent with anxiety disorder

Importantly, the researchers found that among women with a primary diagnosis of depression, 66 percent also had at least one additional diagnosis, most commonly an anxiety disorder. Another important finding was that 22.6 percent of the women with a positive screen for depression were determined to have bipolar disorder through the diagnostic assessment. In other words, nearly one in four women flagged with "postpartum depression" actually had bipolar disorder. This can occur because depressive symptoms are a part of bipolar disorder. As such, a person may primarily experience depression, and they (and their provider) may not recognize periods of (hypo)mania indicative of bipolar disorder. This is significant because treatment geared toward bipolar disorder would be indicated rather than standard depression treatments.

Source: Sarah Chai / Pexels

Lastly, thoughts of self-harm in this population are not rare. Among the women screened, 3.2 percent reported some degree of self-harm ideation, with higher rates (19.3 percent) among women who screened positive for depression.

The perinatal period is a vulnerable time for new onset and recurrence of psychiatric illness, with as many as one in five women experiencing a perinatal mood and anxiety disorder. The findings of this study highlight that there is no single timeline or experience that defines perinatal mental health. As such, follow-up clinical assessment and discussions are required because symptoms can overlap. Feeling sad, overwhelmed, unable to enjoy things, or unable to sleep can occur in perinatal depression as well as other mental health conditions. Proper diagnosis can help guide appropriate treatment and support.

item.title: Food Traps as Play
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Food Traps as Play

Gamifying consumption and fun eating.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • “Advergames” draw children into product loyalty.
  • Celebrities endorse energy-rich, nutrition-poor, sugary foods.
  • Critics call these efforts the “construction of fun” and denounce them as predatory.

Many decades before clever marketers printed QR codes on the backs of sugary breakfast cereal boxes that opened the cyber door to mesmerizing promotional product tie-in video games, radio dramas attracted kids with publicity puzzles.

Fans of the delightfully narrated film A Christmas Story will remember how young Ralphie, the main character, faithfully tuned in to his weekly cliff-hanger radio drama, Little Orphan Annie, to listen to encrypted clues. He used his “Little Orphan Annie Secret Decoder Pin” to unlock a message that only devoted followers could read.

Forty-foot-tall leg-lamp sculpture, Chickasha, Oklahoma, inspired by the “major award” in the film "A Christmas Story."
Source: Image courtesy TulGuy via Wikimedia Commons, 2025, Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication.

His decryption had demanded preparation. Ralphie had needed to mail to the show’s sponsor little foil tabs that came inside boxes of the chocolaty drink-mix, the once-famous Ovaltine. Ovaltine, initially styled as medicinal by the Swiss chemist who devised the mixture, combined malted barley, powdered eggs, and cocoa into a not-so-tasty yeast-flavored formula meant to beef up skinny kids and to restore recuperating adults.

Ralphie drank his share, and when he had accumulated enough of the tabs and mailed them in, he effectively joined the “Radio Orphan Annie Secret Society.” Then the company would send their secret agent a brass decoder decryption device about the size of a half-dollar. With this premium in hand, keen listeners to Little Orphan Annie, like Ralphie, could decrypt a clandestine message. (Though the story comes from the writer Jean Shepherd’s fictionalized autobiography, the promotion and this little machine were a real thing between 1935 and 1940.)

Ralphie recorded the encoded message number by number, and then deciphered it, twisting the dial on the cipher machine to reveal it letter by letter. Once unraveled and assembled, the text proved not to be about spies and their plots or crooks and their dirty deeds; instead it read: “Be sure to drink your Ovaltine!” The film’s narrator, Jean Shepherd himself, in fact, summed up his young alter-ego’s sense of outrage at having been suckered: “It was a crummy commercial!”

Gamified Promotions

Modern gamified promotions don’t depend upon laying such elaborate, prolonged groundwork because they are only a click away when accessed from a cell phone camera. This instant reward of the current “advergame” is a magnitude cleverer because it reinforces the brand message while one is eating the product.

One of the most intriguing is a new simulated experience offered by the manufacturers of Lucky Charms, long a friendly character-driven product that appealed to kids not just for the sugar jolt it delivered in toy-like marshmallow shapes but for the storyline it perpetuated. (The venerable tag-line, endorsed by a cartoon leprechaun in TV commercials, had promised that kids at breakfast would find the cereal “magically delicious.”) The new strategy, a “Journey to the Gems,” far surpasses that appeal, promising that “consumers can harness the power of the new Lucky Charms Magic Gem charms—which have been stowed away in the goblin den for centuries—to see in the (virtual) dark with rainbow vision and even unlock the change to give their local park an LED lights glow-up.” The power. The goblin den. The dark. The rainbow vision. Gem charms. Nummmm.

Another adventure in brand-loyalty comes from General Foods in a collaboration with a candy brand that is described in the industry publication Hypebeast as the “fan-favorite chocolate and peanut butter cereal.” Players “must crunch the puffs as they fall from the sky.” And one more that is more ambitious and contagious: for its Coco Pops cereal sold in the Middle East, Kellogg’s offered a virtual “jungle experience” accessible through smartphones, and invited kids to compete with their friends on social media, meaning to draw in more consumers. In this game, “web face tracking technology” invites kids to simulate trying on “exotic themed headdresses” that recruit the characters that appear on the cereal boxes.

The Bright Predatory Gaze

The brightly colored graphics on the boxes themselves, not incidentally, are so designed that the playful mascots pictured—the playful tiger, the quirky sea captain, the silly rabbit, the threesome of elves—gaze slightly downward at potential consumers, making eye contact with children, peering down from their perch on the lower grocery store shelves.

The Construction of Fun

Critics call these efforts the “construction of fun” and denounce them as predatory. Besides featuring compelling gamified appeal, these “happy eating” campaigns, as detractors call them, offer products that hold three things in common: high sugar content, near-zero fiber, and highly processed grains. And these ingredients, allied with clever psychology and food chemistry, are designed not so much to respond to a need, hunger, but to prompt consumers to yield to an impulse, our natural craving both for sugar and for play.

In a previous piece, I described how food chemists, neuroscientists, and marketers have collaborated to design snack foods to appeal to consumers. Food chemists now engineer an ultra-palatable mix of sugar, salt, fat, and acid to trigger the munchers’ food circuitry. An influential psychophysicist termed this the “bliss point.”

Crucially, the point of gustatory bliss did not entail satisfaction. In fact, the products are timed to release flavor in the mouth in such a way as to tantalize rather than satisfy. And the engineers did not overlook the opportunity to engineer a pleasurable crunch in the process. One potato chip marketing campaign challenged snackers with the line “betcha can’t eat just one.” They won the bet.

Change a few verbs in this account—collaborate to “plot,” appeal to “trap,” consumers to “targets,” and the marketing scheme, free for all to see, reads like a conspiracy theory.

Celebrity Endorsements, Counterfeit Friends, and Empty Calories

Advertising campaigns recruit famous sports figures to help sell products that are “energy dense” but “nutritionally poor.” LeBron James, who played brilliant basketball for Cleveland, Miami, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia, helps marketers sell sweetened soda to teenage admirers. Peyton Manning, the standout quarterback for the Colts and the Broncos, also endorsed soda. He added high-calorie breakfast cereal to his portfolio.

To hawk these products to impressionable teenagers, celebrity athletes establish one-sided, unreciprocal, distant “parasocial relationships” that may fairly be called “fake.”

Ralphie obsessively followed the game and eventually figured out the trick without being especially fond of Ovaltine. Now consumers semi-consciously equate the sweet soft drink with the star, absorbing some of his mojo with every swig of empty calories.

item.title: Scientists Discovered a New Penguin Species—or Did They?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Scientists Discovered a New Penguin Species—or Did They?

Science communication can sometimes blur the line between hype and truth.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • New "penguin species" headlines are misleading; it's a genetic distinction in known gentoos.
  • Determining distinct species is challenging, often involving reclassification of known animals.
  • Scientific hype can still raise awareness of endangered wildlife and aid in preservation efforts.
New penguins discovered?
Source: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International license. Attribution: Antoine Lamielle

Last week, several news outlets reported that a new penguin species had been discovered on the Kerguelen Islands, one of the most remote places on Earth.

For instance, BBC Wildlife Magazine featured an article with the headline, "Amazing New Penguin Discovered for First Time in Over 100 Years." And ScienceDaily offered: "Scientists Discover First New Penguin Species in More Than 100 Years." As a penguin enthusiast and philosopher of biology, I was intrigued. But I hate to be the bringer of bad news. It turns out that the news reported was quite exaggerated.

Skimming the news, one may easily come to the conclusion that scientists have, for the very first time, discovered penguins on this island. Its name is Pygoscelis kerguelensis, the Southeastern gentoo. But that’s not quite what the scientists reported in their research article that was already published in April this year. Indeed, seafarers already encountered these gentoo penguins in the 19th century.

What really happened is that the team of scientists showed that the distinct ecological and climate pressures of the Kerguelen Islands led to sufficient genetic changes in this population of gentoo penguins to distinguish them as a fourth distinct species of gentoos.

Challenges in Identifying Species

How to distinguish closely related, yet geographically distinct, populations of animals is one of the major problems in biology—for biology is inevitably blurry. Once, researchers thought there was only one species of gentoo penguins, but the team of scientists argued that we may soon distinguish a fifth species of gentoos on Macquarie Island far to the South of New Zealand.

To the untrained eye, you may not notice any differences between these penguins, but spend more time with them, and you’ll notice slight differences.

When most people hear about the discovery of a new species, they think we’ve come across a species that humans have never seen, or at least not bothered to describe. But most often things are a bit more boring. We’ve just assumed that similar-looking animals were part of the same species and are now learning that this was a mistake. But to get to that point, things can take quite a while.

“For over 100 years, it’s been controversial as to how many species or how many subspecies there are,” says biology professor Rauri Bowie. “There’s probably no species of penguin ... more debated than the gentoo penguin.”

Importance of the Discovery

Nevertheless, I don’t want to be a party pooper. This discovery is still great news. Because of human interference, several penguin species have already gone extinct. I hope this will be a wake-up call to preserve and protect the diversity of gentoo penguins we can find on this planet. A little bit of hype may be excused if it results in people learning to love the natural world.

item.title: Why Do I Write So Many Books?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Why Do I Write So Many Books?

Personal Perspective: For me, writing is a case study in self-motivation.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Writing isn't always a path to fame or wealth, nor its motivation.
  • Writing can build a lasting legacy.
  • Writing often offers intrinsic fulfillment over external rewards or ego boosts.

Since 1997, I have had 40 books published. I have four more that are coming out over the next few months, and two additional ones that are being considered for publication. None of these have been self-published; all of them are from trade publishers, university presses, or scholarly independents.

In addition to my books, all of them non-fiction, I’ve had published a couple dozen articles and more than 200 blog posts like this one. And like most people, I’ve written thousands of emails and, when I had real jobs, lots of memos. (Do people still write memos?) That adds up to millions of words (and doesn’t include the many letters I wrote to friends and family when that was something people actually did).

I say (actually write) this not to boast but to question its motive(s). It’s certainly not “normal” human behavior, making me question why I’ve spent much of the past three decades scribbling away. It’s definitely not for money, as there are far more lucrative occupations to choose if my goal was to get rich. It’s not to try to become well-known, as that is highly unlikely given that my genre is not a particularly popular one. American cultural history, it turns out, is not a great path to fortune or fame.

While there might be a certain kind of romance associated with being an author, I can say that the process itself is considerably less than glamorous. Spending days alone in a room stringing together words, sentences, paragraphs, and chapters to fill a book is a tedious pursuit, especially when knowing you’ll do very much the same thing tomorrow, the day after that, and so on, just with a different combination of letters.

Given the fact that there seems to be no financial- or ego-based motive for my writing, I have to wonder if I suffer from some form of psychological condition that is driving me to spend the majority of my waking life tapping keys. The three possibilities that come to mind are compulsion, obsession, and addiction, each one having its own markers and worth delineating. Definitions of each are thus in order.

Compulsions are repetitive behaviors that individuals feel driven to perform because of persistent thoughts called obsessions. These obsessions can cause anxiety, and engaging in compulsions may offer temporary relief from that distress. Compulsions involve an overwhelming urge to do something but don't create satiation in the brain's reward circuitry.

Obsessions are recurrent, persistent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts, images, or urges that cause anxiety or distress. Obsessions often involve a feared outcome, such as being responsible for harm to oneself or to others, or being seen as unethical, immoral, or imperfect.

Addiction, according to the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM), is a chronic disease that involves compulsively using substances or engaging in behaviors that continue despite harmful consequences. Addiction creates a sense of pleasure in the brain and removes discomfort from cravings.

Given my unusual behavior, do I qualify for any of these conditions? While I might be compelled to write (I’m not completely content unless I produce two clean pages a day and have been known to start a new book on the very same day that I finished another), I suffer from no anxiety, distress, fears, or discomfort associated with the process, which makes me think not. Rather, I see myself along the lines of a bricklayer, laying down word after word to build something that will eventually stand on its own and hopefully last.

While I wouldn’t be averse to having one of my books hit the bestseller list, the pleasure I receive from being a published author is more in the knowledge that I’ve created a body of work that will survive after I’ve written my last word. Unlike many other professions, there is a certain immortality attached to writing, making my books a literal paper (and now digital) trail documenting that I spent some time on the planet.

If professionally diagnosed, psychologists would likely say that I am simply intrinsically motivated versus extrinsically motivated, meaning that, despite its rather grueling nature, I find writing to be at some level personally satisfying rather than a means to reap externally defined rewards. It appears that, in other words, I am driven to write simply because it is who I am and what I do, which, at the end of the day, is good enough for me.

item.title: What You Should Be Doing in Therapy and Probably Aren’t
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

What You Should Be Doing in Therapy and Probably Aren’t

Personal Perspective: I spent years in therapy stalled because of one thing.

Posted October 1, 2026

Source: RDNE Stock Project / Pexel

I won’t say I had the wrong kind of therapist for decades. But I sometimes wonder. What if early on, I had someone who challenged me more? Would I have become confident and secure sooner? Or would I have cowered and become withdrawn?

It probably would have sent me into a ruminating rabbit hole of self-loathing and a tailspin of anxiety. Who needs someone gently pushing you when you’re already masochistically pushing yourself for not measuring up?

Challenging isn’t aggressive confrontation—the put-up-your-dukes confrontation.

It’s an invitation to look at incongruities in human behavior and what they say, want, or believe. It can introduce a different perspective on an issue or help gently explore blind spots. In the right hands and with the right timing, it’s therapeutic gold. It’s essential for creating growth and change. But it’s a delicate skill because if it’s too forceful or done without adequate empathy, it can be received as blame or aggression and cause harm to the therapeutic relationship.1,2

The Skill of Challenging Is an Art

My current therapist, Hard-Ass Andie—she knows I call her that—is excellent. She offers a nuanced balance of empathy and challenge. But a solid foundation of safety and trust was built before she went for the jugular (kidding!) and challenged my thinking, beliefs, or behaviour.

Unfortunately, pre-bipolar disorder diagnosis and in the early stages of recovery, I had too much support and too little confrontation. Because of that, my growth in therapy stalled. But I never thought to talk about goals or progress.

With my first therapist—let’s call her Kim—I had no idea what I should expect from therapy. I had nothing to compare it to. Maybe feeling okay or at least feeling seen and heard for 50 minutes every couple of weeks was as good as it got. Then back to the same old, same old severe depression.

I spent years with Kim, and she never once asked whether the sessions were helping me move towards what I wanted. Hell, I hadn’t really figured out what I wanted. That was one of my issues—I didn’t know what my needs even were.

Appointment after appointment, I confided in her and gained insight. I understood my childhood and my family of origin dynamics, but I hadn’t felt significant change nor had I dropped unwanted behaviours. I graduated from being a very depressed person to a very insightful depressed person.

Breaking Up with My Therapist Was Hard

I invested a lot of time and money into working with Kim. And I liked her. Really liked her. Truth is, I loved her; and I think she had a great deal of affection for me. She was the first person I felt safe with; safe enough to share my darkest thoughts and most vulnerable parts.

I had a lot to risk if I started to question her and the success of our sessions. And what qualified as success? We never defined that. Short-term therapy typically starts with setting goals. But I wasn’t doing short-term therapy. I was all in—for the long haul. I knew my stuff wasn’t going to be resolved in six to eight 50-minute appointments. I don’t know if anyone actually can. But that’s another post.

Yes, she knew what brought me in. I was struggling emotionally and grappling with binge eating. But we never explicitly outlined my goals, and worse, we never established a routine to review whether I was moving towards them. I needed a way to know I wasn’t spinning my wheels. Eventually I realized I was.

For three years, I came to her office at least twice a month and told her I was feeling depressed. Very depressed. We talked about the trauma I experienced, how my parents lacked the basic skills to attune to me (they both had mental illness) and the very trendy topic of the ’90s: the Healing-the-Shame-That-Binds-You-à la-John-Bradshaw shame.

Each week I would go to sessions still depressed, still with suicidal ideation and unmotivated to get out of bed but managing to do so. After months of this, she asked me, “You’re still feeling depressed?”

Um, yeah, that’s what depression is!? Though I didn’t know I had clinical depression at the time. I had felt this way for so long; I took it as my baseline. I was taken aback when she said it. But I didn’t have the confidence to say anything. It was so confusing. I had always felt so supported by her, so safe and cared for. How could she not understand this? Could she be missing something?

If we had talked at the start about what I wanted from therapy and, more pivotal, reviewed at regular intervals whether I was seeing changes, we could have reassessed our approach or explored if she was even the right therapist for me.

But we didn’t.

Get Clear on Goals and Review Them Regularly

Getting clear on goals is important, but even more problematic is not regularly evaluating progress towards them. Ask: “How are we doing? Are we there yet?”

If my counselor and I had held those conversations, the answers would have been ‘not so good and not by a long shot’. I would have had a chance to rethink what I was doing and maybe move on.

© Victoria Maxwell

item.title: Leaving Romania, but Never Fully Leaving Home
item.description:
Grief

Leaving Romania, but Never Fully Leaving Home

The mind often remains at home after migration.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Physical migration does not always mean psychological departure from home.
  • Cognitive immobility traps migrants in mental ties to their homeland, causing unresolved longing.
  • Returning home doesn't always heal emotional separation; it may deepen longing and sadness.

"I left, but my soul stayed here. In my free time, I could think of nothing but home. Even while caring for my baby, my thoughts were always on returning; everyone wondered why I came back. After all, I had it better there than many do here."

Those words were those of Antoanela Andonescu, also affectionately called "Coca." Coca is a geriatric nurse who left her little hometown of Bicaz in eastern Romania to live and work in Italy. She was featured in a DW documentary called "Homesick" that aired June 26, 2026.

Like thousands of other Romanians and millions of people around the world who have left their homeland because of circumstances beyond their control, some leave a part of themselves at home.

Coca’s words echo what a Syrian student interviewed in another study said: "I am still in Syria. My soul is there." That is the reality for many people on the move. According to Coca, during her free time, and whenever she could be by herself, her thoughts always returned to her hometown, Bicaz.

Such thoughts can make a person re-experience their hometown, including family, events, sounds, sights, and smells. Anyone who constantly engages in this mental exercise to find solace and relieve their sense of loss after leaving home and intense longing for it may become trapped in a condition called cognitive immobility. This could lead to sadness, crying, and other serious health issues.

When They Left Romania, Their Souls Remained

According to the documentary, a severe economic crisis, which led to mass layoffs, high unemployment, and widespread hardship, meant that when Romania joined the EU, many Romanians left their homeland. This included young people, Coca and her two sisters among them. But Coca always dreamed of returning. In that sense, she left because of circumstances beyond her control.

"Because of constraints and circumstances beyond people’s control, they may engage in physical migration or departure from a location without engaging in mental migration or departure at the same time, resulting in mental immobility" (Olumba, 2023, 772).

Leaving Bicaz was something Coca felt she could not control, and when she left, as she put it, "her soul stayed." After she left Romania, she first went to Turkey, where she may have experienced the first stage of cognitive immobility, which is the awareness/separation state. This is when a migrant wishes intensely that she had never left and cannot stop herself from re-experiencing the people, sounds, smells, and other things back home when alone. This is better captured by Coca’s words: "In my free time, I could think of nothing but home. Even while caring for my baby, my thoughts were always on returning [home]."

Coca described her life in Turkey as mostly working, saving money, and returning to her hometown with gifts and clothes for her nieces and other family members, while keeping only the basics for herself. She confirmed that her focus was to earn enough money to return to her hometown for such visits.

It was during this period that she may have entered the retrieval stage, a time when she believed that returning would ease the severe longing and sense of loss she felt while in Turkey, without realising that return visits alone could not necessarily end her suffering. The retrieval stage can be the most severe period for someone experiencing this condition.

The DW documentary captured the lived experiences of other Romanians in the Ostia region near Rome. During a gathering around a long table over a meal, one young woman who visited her family members in Italy was asked whether she could move to Italy. She insisted that she could not live there and, crying, said:

"I cannot go to a country that took the person I love most away from me. I do not like it here; I can not fit in here. I would rather stay in Romania and struggle; it is better to stay in Romania than come here and not feel like myself."

As she spoke, she wiped tears from her eyes. I found myself doing the same when I watched and rewatched the clip to write down her words. It can be very difficult for anyone who feels forced to leave their hometown for a strange new place where they may not feel wanted or welcomed. This young woman insisted that she could never feel like herself in Italy. She seemed to be afraid that if she left Romania physically, part of herself might still remain in her hometown.

Another Romanian woman in the documentary described how their lives were torn apart when they first arrived in Italy. They lived at a train station while struggling to find work and somewhere else to sleep. She laughed as she recalled those experiences, perhaps because she now misses parts of that period, even though it was very difficult at the time. She said that she missed everything about her hometown while living in Italy, and, speaking about her desire to return home, said:

"Every time we go back to our country, it is painful for us. Because for years we have been saying over and over again that [it's] 'just one more year'. We say we will stay one more year and then come back. But then we cannot bring ourselves to take that step; we stay. It is very painful, especially saying goodbye, when you just cannot stop crying."

It can be overwhelming for anyone who feels this way. This woman wished to return home for good, but things had not yet worked out as she had planned. Each time she returned to her hometown in Romania for a visit, leaving it again was deeply painful, and she would cry, just as many people experiencing cognitive immobility do. You may cry because you miss the sights, sounds, people, food, smells, and way of life that are familiar to you, and because you are returning to a place and a life that still feels strange and to which you have still to adjust.

Final Thoughts

Coca now runs a care home in her hometown in Romania. Among her patients is her elderly father, who used to work in one of the local factories before the company collapsed. Her sister also returned to join her. Coca could be in the stabilisation stage of cognitive immobility because she is no longer seeking to recover what was lost but is creating new value in the place she calls home.

By helping local residents, including her father, live more comfortably in their later years, Coca is also helping herself and inspiring others who may be considering a return to their hometown. Anyone who has left their hometown may understand how painful it can be to live with the wish that they had never left in the first place.

Coca and her sister were able to return, but not everyone can. For some people, home may be too far away, unsafe, changed beyond recognition, or no longer available in the form they remember. Addressing this problem may require finding a way to remain connected to what was lost without allowing that loss to consume life in the present.

item.title: The Riveting Story of the Damaged Lives of Big Captive Cats
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

The Riveting Story of the Damaged Lives of Big Captive Cats

Carol Bradley offers a detailed story of abuse, rescue, and hope.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • The book "Striped Reckoning" is a fact-filled story of the lives and rescue of big captive cats.
  • She writes about the astonishing brutal mistreatment of lions, tigers, and other big cats in America.
  • She also tells how sanctuaries rescue and rehabilitate these suffering animals.
Source: alena Evseenko/Pexels.

It's well-known that the lives of large captive animals can be highly compromised. Because of mass media, numerous people now know the story of the horrific lives of captive big cats kept in zoos, circuses, backyards, homes, and TV and movie sets and the sordid stories of Tiger Kings' Joe Exotic and others, including Tim Stark and Jeff Lowe all of whom were eventually put out of business.

I have found it very difficult to put together the complicated puzzle of how this all happened, and in her long-awaited highly acclaimed new book aptly titled Striped Reckoning: Tiger Kings and the Battle to Rescue America’s Captive Big Cats Big, award-winning author Carol Bradley beautifully assembles the main pieces into an understandable, coherent whole. Animal advocate or not, people have been moved by the tireless efforts to free these animals and regardless of one's stance on animal ethics, I'm sure Bradley's book will be an eye-opening read.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Striped Reckoning and how did you come up with the title?

Carol Bradley: The idea for this book came to me while I was attending the Performing Animal Welfare Society’s (PAWS) International Captive Wildlife Conference several years ago. There I watched a video of a tiny tiger cub being forced to swim in a pool at a roadside zoo in Florida. The cub was named Ariel, and she suffered from some kind of neurological issue; she could barely keep her head out of the water. I came home haunted by the sight of that sweet little cub struggling in vain to keep her head up. But at the time I wasn’t sure readers would be drawn to a book about captive big cats in the U.S. Besides, I was working on another book, so I set the idea aside.

Two years after that, I learned that a zookeeper in Oklahoma had just been sentenced to prison for shooting to death a handful of tigers and also, mainly, for trying to hire a hit man to murder his nemesis, a sanctuary owner in Florida who had been working overtime to drive him out of business. Suddenly, I had a hook for a book. I immediately began diving into the history of captive big cats in the U.S. Two months later, Netflix came out with “Tiger King: Murder, Mayhem and Madness” and overnight that Oklahoma zookeeper, Joe Exotic, became a household name. But much of the story of captive big cats in the U.S. remained untold and that is what I set out to do.

The title of my book refers to the reversal of fortunes: the tigers abused by Exotic and two other so-called Tiger Kings are now enjoying much better lives, while two of the Tiger Kings are out of business and Exotic is behind bars—in a cage of his own making. The tiger on the cover, Luna, was one of the cubs forced to swim at that roadside zoo in Florida. She was rescued and able to spend her final years at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge in Arkansas. Sadly, she died a few weeks before my book was published.

Source: University of Nebraska Press/with permission.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

CB: I first became aware of the poor treatment of animals 23 years ago when, as a newspaper reporter, I covered an egregious puppy mill bust involving a couple trying to enter Montana from Canada, hauling 180 malnourished and shivering collies stacked three deep in the back of a tractor trailer. That case was life-changing for me. After a fellowship at Harvard where I studied animal law, I began writing stories of animal mistreatment in this country. Striped Reckoning is my fourth book.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

CB: The history of tigers and other big cats in America has been an open secret, one that will shock readers who have never given much thought to the animals they may have seen at roadside zoos or performing in movies and circuses. I hope this book will appeal to some of the 64 million people who watched Netflix’s “Tiger King” and to animal lovers everywhere.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

CB: I’ve written exposes of puppy miles, elephants in circuses, the dark days of Hollywood when horses were deliberately tripped to make it look as though they’d fallen in combat, and now this book. I hope readers come away realizing that the laws governing animal care in the U.S. are woefully inadequate. It’s not natural to expect an elephant or a tiger to live in the back of a tractor trailer and be trucked across the country to perform in a center ring, or, in the case of big cats, to be warehoused in small metal cages and bred over and over, denied any semblance of a natural life, yet all of that is allowed. The good news is that breeders are no longer allowed to offer cub-petting, which takes away their incentive for over-breeding. Nevertheless, the U.S. is behind many other countries when it comes to animal welfare.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

Much has been written about big cats’ struggle to survive in the wild. Striped Reckoning focuses on tigers, lions and other big cats that are right here in the U.S. Most readers who have encountered exotic big cats have done so because the animals were being held in captivity. The wretched lives they led and the efforts undertaken to save them deserve to be told.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about this horrific situation they will do something to stop things like this from happening again and treat these magnificent sentient beings with more respect, compassion, and dignity?

CB: Yes, absolutely. I hope to reach people who have never considered what it must be like for a big cat to perform alongside a human being – the declawing, the defanging, and the beatings they have had to endure in order to perform on stage, or the misery they experience never having had the freedom to wander about in nature. And I hope to raise awareness of the sanctuaries that have taken these big cats in, treated their medical issues, and given them better lives.

item.title: Agency Is the New Citizenship
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Agency Is the New Citizenship

Why we need to feel that our action matters to get involved In climate action.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Humans are inclined to act only when we believe our actions matter.
  • Cognitive and ecological systems are becoming increasingly entangled.
  • Agency is our capacity to participate consciously in shaping systems that simultaneously shape us.
Agency is becoming a defining capability of 21st-century citizenship. It is a scarce resource, that we must cultivate consciously.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

When it comes to climate action, knowledge matters. Communication and attitudes matter. Yet, de facto, humans are only likely to translate these ingredients into climate-friendly intentions when they believe their own actions can make a difference. Self-efficacy amplifies engagement, and to a certain extent it conditions it. Knowledge does not lead naturally to behavior change. Instead, a more complex pathway, in which knowledge feeds engagement, shapes attitudes, and influences intentions, operates.

There is a larger lesson here. Agency is becoming a defining capability of 21st-century citizenship. In a world increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), climate disruption, and the intensifying interaction between the two, the scarcest resource today is not information. We are surrounded by more information than any previous generation could have ever imagined.

What is becoming scarce is human agency: our capacity to understand what is happening, determine what matters, garner the initiative to make meaningful choices, and act upon them.

From informed people to empowered citizens

For much of modern history, citizenship has been associated with rights, responsibilities, and participation in public life. The digital era added another requirement: access to information. The hybrid era demands something deeper.

We increasingly experience reality through technological systems that select, summarize, recommend, predict, and generate. Search engines mediate what we discover. Algorithms determine much of what reaches our attention. Generative AI can formulate arguments, answer questions, and increasingly undertake tasks on our behalf. These capabilities can expand agency enormously. Someone with a smartphone can access knowledge, translate languages, analyze information, and mobilize communities with capacities once reserved for institutions. At the same time, the locus of agency can subtly shift. When machines suggest what to read, how to formulate an argument, where to go, and, eventually, what decision to make, convenience can gradually become cognitive delegation.

In a hybrid context, citizenship acquires a cognitive dimension. Emerging research into generative AI and cognitive offloading shows that the impact of AI on thought and decision-making is not necessarily determined by the frequency of usage, but by whether the tools are used as a replacement for deeper thinking processes. Societies depend on people capable of paying attention, questioning information, tolerating uncertainty, deliberating with others, and understanding the choices they make. Unquestioned AI integration puts these capabilities at risk.

The mind and the planet are interconnected

There is another dimension of the hybrid world that receives (too) little attention. The technologies reshaping our minds have a physical metabolism. AI feels almost immaterial: a question disappears into a screen, and an answer appears seconds later. Behind that exchange sit semiconductors, data centers, cooling systems, transmission networks, minerals, electricity, water, and land. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centers consumed around 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, approximately 1.5 percent of global electricity consumption, with demand projected to more than double by 2030. Their environmental consequences depend heavily on where they are built, how efficiently they operate, and how their electricity is generated. This exposes a defining feature of our emerging reality: cognitive and ecological systems are becoming increasingly entangled.

Individual digital actions appear insignificant. Yet billions of them generate a gigantic rise in infrastructure demand. In turn, that infrastructure requires capital, energy, water, minerals, and land. And those demands affect ecosystems and communities that are already under strain. Environmental disruption, in turn, influences health, livelihoods, migration, politics, and the information environments through which societies understand those disruptions. Technology affects the mind. The mind shapes behavior. Behavior influences markets and institutions. Those systems shape technology and the planet. And the planet determines the conditions within which human life is possible. Treating “digital transformation” and “environmental sustainability” as separate agendas makes increasingly zero sense.

Beyond the consumer

Climate-engagement research focuses on consumers and demonstrates why engagement matters for sustainable consumption. Yet the hybrid world requires another step: from consumer agency to citizen agency. A consumer chooses among options presented by a system. A citizen can question and influence the system itself. That distinction matters because many consequential decisions surrounding AI and planetary health occur upstream: how data centers are powered and located, which technologies receive investment, what environmental costs companies disclose, how algorithms are designed, what governments regulate, what schools teach, and what societies decide constitutes progress.

Agency consequently operates across interconnected scales. At the micro level, it means retaining command over attention, judgment, and choice. At the meso level, families, schools, workplaces, and communities establish norms determining where technology assists and where humans deliberately remain in command. At the macro level, governments and markets shape infrastructure, incentives, and rules. At the meta level, societies confront the deeper question of what kind of future they are building. Citizenship is the connective tissue between these levels.

From artificial to hybrid intelligence

The objective is neither technological retreat nor frictionless automation. It is hybrid intelligence: cultivating the relationship between natural and artificial intelligence so technology expands human possibility while humans retain the capacity and responsibility to choose. This requires double literacy: Algorithmic literacy enables us to understand what machines can do, how to use them, and where their limitations lie, but, most importantly, how they influence our own ability to think. Human literacy cultivates critical thinking, compassion, self-awareness, creativity, moral reasoning, and the ability to connect decisions with their consequences for ourselves, others, and the living world. Agency converts these literacies into citizenship.

The connection with planetary health is unsettling. Someone who understands climate change but feels powerless may disengage. Someone technologically empowered but unable to perceive the ecological consequences of technological choices may inadvertently intensify the problem. Flourishing requires capacity alongside consciousness. Agency is therefore more than personal autonomy. It is our capacity to participate consciously in shaping systems that simultaneously shape us.

The A-frame: agency in action

When everything appears connected, individual action can seem insignificant. Agency begins with a different premise: No person controls the whole system, yet everyone participates in it. Four practices can help translate that understanding into everyday citizenship.

Awareness: What is shaping me? Notice the technological, social, economic, and ecological forces surrounding a choice. Ask what an algorithm is doing, what information is absent, where your attention is being directed, and what physical resources lie behind seemingly weightless digital services.

Appreciation: What is worth preserving? Use technology for what it does well while recognizing the value of natural intelligence: judgment, imagination, empathy, relationships, embodied experience, and our dependence on living systems.

Acceptance: What are the limits? Recognize uncertainty and constraint. AI can be wrong. Individual climate choices cannot resolve structural problems alone. Natural resources are finite. Acknowledging limits enables more intelligent action within them.

Accountability: What will I do? Move from knowing to choosing. Ask who benefits, who bears the cost, what consequences extend beyond the immediate transaction, and what remains your responsibility when technology assists you.

In a nutshell: Humans are inclined to act only when we believe our actions matter. In the hybrid world, we are simultaneously users of technology, citizens of societies, and inhabitants of a living planet. The future will emerge from billions of interactions between natural and artificial intelligence. Whether those interactions contribute to hybrid flourishing depends, in no small measure, on whether each of us remains a conscious agent behind the scenes.

item.title: The Job of a Toy Analyst
item.description:
Psych Careers

The Job of a Toy Analyst

A psychological analysis of play.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Play isn't just for kids. It supports mental health, creativity, and well-being across the entire lifespan.
  • Everyday objects can hold memory, carry deep meaning, and express who we are.
  • A beloved doll can be a psychological tool, helping adults process grief and stay connected to loved ones.
Author's Personal Research Collection
Source: Peter Danzig/Personal Collection

I so often get questions from the public or my colleagues in the field asking, What is it that you do? What is a Toy & Pop Culture Analyst? Is that a real job? Do you play with the toys or display them?

There’s a range of answers to this question, but let’s start at the beginning. Throughout the lifespan, researchers have noted, play is critical to mental health, creativity, cognitive flexibility, and well-being. And yet, we often view toys as being only for children. That is where the disconnect is for the general public, but also the toy industry. In recent years, post pandemic, the nostalgia boom across industries has certainly centered play and longing for simpler times as adults now have surpassed children in collecting and purchasing toys.

For me, it’s not that adults have surpassed the key demographics and that this discovery warrants longitudinal research but that we collectively have designated toy play as child development, excluding key research and also simply excluding an audience through the microaggression that as we age, play is designated to vacations, social outings, or job satisfaction, ignoring the critical elements that material culture research have often shown us: that items hold meaning and are a form of expression.

That is where my job comes in. I research national trends of play and creativity over the lifespan and also work with companies, marketing professionals, toy designers, and culture outlets to advise how toys and play can be incredibly lucrative while also being inclusive of various audiences. Questions such as, Do dolls need to be sold as a girls item or can we be more gender expansive, and simply have the toy isle and product line sold as dolls for all people? Can toys marketed at adults capture the essence of collectability while also scaling design and materials to match an adult collector’s excitement for expression? Even ensuring companies consider questions about including audiences in their toy lines through lived experiences, such as people living with a disability, gender inclusion, and race and ethnicity as culturally humble approaches to the designs and characters they are marketing. It’s not all fun and games, but it’s quite endearing, more so when I walk into a toy aisle and see the work translated into something children and adults alike can explore. But it also shows up in personal ways, which is my why when it comes to this work.

Recently, upon Dolly Parton’s death, I felt a great deal of disenfranchised grief and mourning, and I of course displayed her records and played them as I contemplated her legacy, but also, there were Funko Pops, a mug, and most importantly, a doll my late father purchased my mother of Dolly Parton at a toy show in the 1990s. As a child I was in awe of it, and as an adult, displaying it brought me a sense of peace in the loss of Dolly, but so did remembering my father’s love of play and my mother’s inclusive approach to dolls, noting toys are for play, not for restricting us. In considering my work as a toy analyst, this doll is a piece of material culture that resonates with me in various parts of my life and brings me comfort. While most may consider the doll itself as for children, I’d consider it a psychological tool for transferring my emotions to and through it to better understand my world. Winnicott's work on transitional objects, and how it extends into adulthood, is a core part of toy analysis and understanding.

This is a small example of the many ways toy analysts examine the world around us or work with companies to better understand the intention and impacts of play. There are very few researchers and professional toy analysts, as the field is somewhat multidisciplinary between marketing, psychology, social stigma, and growing shifts in social psychology toward inclusion.

I hope today that you may stroll through the toy aisle, garage, attic, flea market, toy show, or local comic shop and allow yourself to shed what social stigma or fear you have of judgment, and allow yourself to find play, model for yourself and others what form your adventure can take, be it a small knick-knack on your work desk, or a carefully curated collection of thousands of action figures, dolls, die-cast cars, or games. The point is not to weed out joy, but to weed in what it could look like for you to engage with toys as they were always meant to be: for creativity, neurodevelopment, or simply expression.

Mary Poppins Vintage Mattel doll and Vintage Book
Source: Peter Andrew Danzig

Today, I think I’ll pop open this vintage Mary Poppins book on a cold, rainy Monday while taking a moment to enjoy the vintage Mattel Mary Poppins doll I had as a child, which now brings a sense of warmth as a display item. My sense of play has grown, but adults don’t need to “grow up and out” of it; we simply need to allow ourselves to evolve with play. As we do, the world shifts in our collective ideas of what toys can do, and maybe, just maybe, toy analysts can then find even more ways to research and open doors for us all. For today, let’s simply play. Don’t toy with me is my favorite saying, and now I think you may see why.
